title: 4  Diagnosing Markov Chains
text:
4.1 Inspecting a run
A Markov chain can have the right stationary distribution and still give a poor estimate after a thousand iterations. It may spend much of that time near its starting point, move slowly through the distribution, or explore only one of several regions. The convergence results of Chapter 3 describe what happens as a run grows indefinitely. In practice, we run a chain for a limited number of iterations and must decide whether the resulting estimates are accurate enough.
Suppose two chains each produce 20,000 values from a standard Normal target. Both aim at a distribution with mean zero and standard deviation one. If we repeated both simulations, would their averages vary equally much from run to run? And if one average is 0.04, is that a reason to worry? We will use this simple target to investigate what a chain’s behavior tells us about the accuracy of its estimates.
We will then apply the same reasoning to a Bayesian analysis: estimating the proportion of Dutch-language songs on a radio station. There, we will need to judge the precision of a posterior mean and a credible interval. The central question throughout is how much confidence we can place in a finite simulation.
Run the following setup before working through the examples. We use tidyverse to organize and summarize the draws, posterior to calculate diagnostics, and bayesplot and patchwork to draw and combine the plots. The rstan package fits the radio model later in the chapter.
We begin with the Normal transition rule from Chapter 3. At each step, combine part of the current value with a new random draw: \[
\theta^{(t+1)}=\phi\theta^{(t)}+\sqrt{1-\phi^2}\,\varepsilon_t,
\qquad \varepsilon_t\sim\text{N}(0,1).
\] Each new \(\varepsilon_t\) is drawn independently. The parameter \(\phi\), with \(-1<\phi<1\), controls how much of the current value carries over to the next. With \(\phi=0\), the next value is a fresh standard Normal draw. With \(\phi\) close to one, successive values tend to stay close together. This rule is called a first-order autoregressive process, or AR(1) process.
These choices of \(\phi\) preserve the same standard Normal target. To check this, suppose the current state is standard Normal. A weighted sum of independent Normal variables is also Normal, as we saw in Chapter 3. The next state has mean zero and variance \[
\phi^2\times1+(1-\phi^2)\times1=1.
\] It is therefore standard Normal too. Changing \(\phi\) changes how the chain moves, while keeping its stationary distribution fixed.
The following function stores \(N\) states, including the initial state in theta[1], and makes \(N-1\) transitions:
ar1_chain <- function(phi, N, init = 0) {
  theta <- numeric(N)
  theta[1] <- init
  for (t in seq_len(N - 1)) {
    theta[t + 1] <- phi * theta[t] + sqrt(1 - phi^2) * rnorm(1)
  }
  theta
}
We generate three chains, with \(\phi=0\), \(0.5\), and \(0.95\). Each starts with a draw from the target, so its distribution is stationary from the start. This lets us study dependence without also introducing an effect of a fixed starting point.
phis <- c(0, 0.5, 0.95)
N_ar1 <- 20000
ar1_chains <- lapply(phis, function(phi) {
  ar1_chain(phi, N_ar1, init = rnorm(1))
})
A trace plot shows the sampled values in the order they were produced. In Figure 4.1, the three chains all fluctuate around zero, but they do so quite differently.
Figure 4.1: The first 500 iterations of three chains that all have the N(0, 1) stationary distribution. With \(\phi = 0\) the draws are independent. With \(\phi = 0.95\) the chain wanders slowly, and a short window can give an unrepresentative picture of the target.
With \(\phi=0\), values move frequently between the two sides of zero. Most lie near the center, with occasional values farther away, as we expect for a standard Normal distribution. This is useful behavior when estimating the mean: the run samples both sides without spending long stretches on either one. With \(\phi=0.95\), values tend to stay above or below zero for stretches of time. This chain has the same standard Normal stationary distribution, but a short stretch may contain mostly positive or mostly negative values. Its average can therefore be far from zero.

title: 4  Diagnosing Markov Chains
text:
4.1.1 The starting point
So far we have drawn the initial state from the target. Usually we cannot do that: obtaining posterior draws is the problem we are trying to solve. Instead, we choose a starting value and let the chain move from there. What happens if that value is far from the region where most of the target probability lies?
Consider four chains with \(\phi=0.99\), started at \(-6\), \(-3\), \(3\), and \(6\). The standard Normal target puts most of its probability between \(-2\) and \(2\). Figure 4.2 shows how these chains move from their starts toward that region.








Figure 4.2: Four AR(1) chains with phi = 0.99, started at -6, -3, 3, and 6. The shaded band marks the interval from -2 to 2. Early values reflect the chosen starting points; later values fluctuate through a similar region.





Early values can pull the estimated mean toward the starting point. Burn-in is the practice of discarding an initial part of the run to reduce this influence. A trace plot can reveal that early values are still moving away from the starting point. It cannot establish exactly when the effect of initialization has become negligible.
Some sampling algorithms also adjust their settings during an initial warm-up phase. Stan, which we use later in this chapter, does this. Its warm-up therefore serves two purposes: allowing movement away from the start and learning suitable sampling settings. Posterior summaries use the subsequent phase, with those settings fixed.


4.1.2 Warning patterns
The same questions arise with a posterior whose shape we do not know. Does the chain keep drifting? Does it remain near one value for long stretches? Do different chains explore different regions? Figure 4.3 illustrates these three patterns on a proportion scale.








Figure 4.3: Three exaggerated synthetic warning patterns. Top: upward drift. Middle: repeated values and slow movement. Bottom: different centers across records. Real sampling problems can be much subtler, as in the exercises.





In the trend example, later values are consistently higher than earlier values, so the average depends strongly on where we stop. In the sticking example, long flat stretches contribute little new information. In the disagreement example, each record looks stable on its own, but the records give different answers about where the distribution lies.
These are deliberately constructed illustrations. The first adds an upward trend to random fluctuations. The second usually repeats its previous value and occasionally moves. The third generates values around two different centers. Their purpose is to make the warning patterns easy to recognize; the exercises contain subtler examples.
For an actual sampler, the pattern guides the next step. A chain still moving away from its start may need more warm-up. Slow movement may call for different sampling settings. Persistent separation between chains calls for investigation of why they are not exploring the same regions. We will encounter these problems when we build samplers in the coming chapters.


Quiz yourself!

A friend runs one very long chain of 100,000 iterations rather than four chains of 25,000. Their trace plot is a flat band of noise and they conclude that the chain has converged. Which of the three warning patterns could their design not have detected, and why?

title: 4  Diagnosing Markov Chains
section: 4.2 Dependence and the accuracy of an average
text:
4.2 Dependence and the accuracy of an average
Consecutive draws in a Markov chain are usually correlated: Where the chain is now tells you something about where it will be next. A chain in which that correlation dies away quickly is said to mix well; a chain that stays correlated over many iterations mixes poorly. Mixing affects how precisely we can estimate posterior summaries from a chain of a given length.

4.2.1 How far does the dependence persist?
The AR(1) traces show that nearby values can resemble one another. Compare each value with the next one, then with the value two steps later, and so on. The separation is called the lag. Lag 1 compares neighbors; lag 10 compares values ten iterations apart. The correlation at a given lag is called autocorrelation.
For a stationary chain, the lag-\(k\) autocorrelation is \[
\rho_k=\operatorname{Corr}(\theta^{(t)},\theta^{(t+k)}).
\] A value near one means that high values tend to be followed by high values, and low values by low values, at that lag. A negative value indicates a tendency to lie on opposite sides of the mean. The autocorrelation function (ACF) plots these correlations against the lag.
For our AR(1) process, \(\rho_k=\phi^k\): each step carries forward a fraction \(\phi\) of the preceding state. Thus when \(\phi=0.95\), lag-one correlation is 0.95, lag-two correlation is \(0.95^2\), and lag-ten correlation is \(0.95^{10}\approx0.60\). Values ten steps apart still tend to resemble each other.
R estimates the autocorrelations from a simulated chain with acf(). For example, acf(ar1_chains[[3]]) plots them for the chain with \(\phi=0.95\). Figure 4.4 compares all three chains.








Figure 4.4: Estimated autocorrelations of the three Normal chains. Dependence disappears immediately when phi = 0, falls quickly when phi = 0.5, and persists across many lags when phi = 0.95. Lag zero compares every value with itself and therefore has correlation one.







4.2.2 Repeating the simulation
To see what this means for an estimate, imagine repeating each simulation 200 times and recording its average each time. We use 2,000 states per run, drawing each initial state from the standard Normal target. The target mean is zero; the spread of the 200 averages tells us how precisely each type of chain estimates it. Each value in the histograms below is an average from a whole run.
The calculation for \(\phi=0.95\) is:

set.seed(48105)
means_95 <- replicate(200, mean(ar1_chain(0.95, 2000, init = rnorm(1))))

Figure 4.5 compares these averages with those from \(\phi=0\) and \(\phi=0.5\).








Figure 4.5: Estimated means from 200 independent runs for each value of phi, with 2,000 states per run. All three sets of estimates are centered near the true mean, zero, but stronger dependence gives more variation between runs. The same horizontal scale is used in all panels.





The chain with \(\phi=0.95\) can spend a substantial part of a run above or below zero. Its average therefore varies much more between runs than the average of independent draws. Each run contains the same number of values, but the resulting estimates are not equally precise. This is the cost of positive autocorrelation.

title: 4  Diagnosing Markov Chains
section: 4.3 Effective sample size and Monte Carlo standard error
text:
4.3 Effective sample size and Monte Carlo standard error
Suppose we estimate a target mean \(\mu\) by the average of \(N\) states, \[
\bar\theta=\frac1N\sum_{t=0}^{N-1}\theta^{(t)}.
\] For independent draws, Chapter 1 gave \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar\theta)=\sigma^2/N\), where \(\sigma^2\) is the target variance. With positively correlated draws, neighboring values often pull the average in the same direction. The covariance terms account for this shared movement and increase the variance of the average.
For a stationary chain, the corresponding large-\(N\) approximation is \[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar\theta)\approx\frac{\sigma^2}{N}
\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\rho_k\right).
\tag{4.1}\] This assumes a finite target variance and autocorrelations that die away fast enough for their sum to be finite. The factor in parentheses describes the effect of dependence. For independent draws, all the \(\rho_k\) are zero and the factor is one. Positive autocorrelations make it larger.
We can express this loss of precision as an effective sample size (ESS): the number of independent draws that would give approximately the same spread of estimated means across repeated runs. Writing \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar\theta)\approx\sigma^2/N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) gives \[
N_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{N}{1+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\rho_k}.
\] For the AR(1) chain, \(\rho_k=\phi^k\). Summing the geometric series gives \[
N_{\mathrm{eff}}
\approx\frac{N}{1+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\phi^k}
=\frac{N}{1+2\phi/(1-\phi)}
=N\frac{1-\phi}{1+\phi}.
\] With \(\phi=0.95\), our 20,000-state chain has an effective sample size of approximately \(20{,}000\times0.05/1.95\approx513\). Its average is about as precise as an average of 513 independent standard Normal draws.
In most applications we do not know the autocorrelations. The function ess_basic() in the posterior package estimates ESS from the sampled values. Compare those estimates with the known AR(1) formula:

tibble(phi = phis,
       ess_formula = N_ar1 * (1 - phi) / (1 + phi),
       ess_estimated = sapply(ar1_chains, ess_basic))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>     phi ess_formula ess_estimated
#>   <dbl>       <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1  0         20000         19078.
#> 2  0.5        6667.         6692.
#> 3  0.95        513.          555.

The columns need not agree exactly. The formula uses known correlations and a long-run approximation; the function uses correlations estimated from a particular path. Repeating the simulation gives different ESS estimates, especially when dependence is strong. Section C.1 derives the exact variance for a chain of \(N\) states and explains the approximation.

4.3.1 Expressing precision in the units of the estimate
ESS tells us how much precision we have relative to independent sampling. To express that precision in the units of the mean, take the square root of its variance: \[
\operatorname{MCSE}(\bar\theta)\approx\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}}.
\tag{4.2}\] This is the Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE). It estimates the standard deviation of the averages we would obtain across repeated runs, as illustrated in Figure 4.5.
For the standard Normal target, \(\sigma=1\). The three 20,000-state runs therefore have approximate MCSEs of \(1/\sqrt{20{,}000}=0.007\) when \(\phi=0\), \(1/\sqrt{6{,}667}=0.012\) when \(\phi=0.5\), and \(1/\sqrt{513}=0.044\) when \(\phi=0.95\).
An estimated mean of 0.04 is thus less than one MCSE from zero for the slowest chain, but more than five MCSEs away for independent draws. An error of 0.04 would thus be quite ordinary for the slowest chain and unusual for independent draws. mcse_mean() estimates the MCSE from the draws:

tibble(phi = phis,
       estimated_mean = sapply(ar1_chains, mean),
       mcse = sapply(ar1_chains, mcse_mean))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>     phi estimated_mean    mcse
#>   <dbl>          <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1  0          -0.00160 0.00721
#> 2  0.5        -0.0211  0.0122 
#> 3  0.95        0.0517  0.0417

An MCSE is not a bound on the error in one run. Differences of one or two MCSEs from the target mean are unsurprising, and larger differences sometimes occur. We use MCSE to judge the expected scale of numerical error and to decide whether further simulation is worthwhile.
Suppose we need an MCSE of 0.02 for the Normal mean. We need approximately \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}=(1/0.02)^2=2{,}500\). For \(\phi=0.95\), this requires \[
N\approx2{,}500\frac{1+0.95}{1-0.95}=97{,}500
\] stored states. Our current 20,000-state run is too short for that purpose. With \(\phi=0.5\), the same target precision requires about 7,500 states. Improving mixing can therefore save substantial computation.
More generally, when the sampler’s behavior stays similar, multiplying the retained run length by four approximately halves the MCSE. A pilot run with MCSE \(e\) suggests multiplying its length by \((e/e_{\mathrm{target}})^2\), where \(e_{\mathrm{target}}\) is the MCSE we want to achieve. This is a planning estimate: check the MCSE again after the longer run.


4.3.2 Would thinning help?
The chain with \(\phi=0.95\) is highly correlated at lag 1 but less so at lag 10, since \(0.95^{10}\approx0.60\). That suggests a fix: Keep every tenth draw and throw the rest away. The retained draws are less correlated, so surely they are better? This is called thinning.
But lower correlation is only part of the comparison. We also have fewer draws. The values we discard were correlated with their neighbors, but they still contributed to estimating the target mean. After keeping every tenth value, we have 2,000 states with lag-one correlation \(0.95^{10}\). Their theoretical ESS is \[
2{,}000\frac{1-0.95^{10}}{1+0.95^{10}}\approx502,
\] slightly below the full run’s ESS of 513. The two effects nearly cancel, leaving a slightly less precise average.
We can make the same comparison with estimated ESS:

theta_95 <- ar1_chains[[3]]
c(full = ess_basic(theta_95),
  thinned = ess_basic(theta_95[seq(1, N_ar1, by = 10)]))
#>     full  thinned 
#> 555.1623 516.1334

An estimated ESS can occasionally be larger after thinning because it is itself estimated with noise. In this example, the theoretical ESS decreases slightly. A practical reason to thin is storage: retaining every value can be costly in a large model. Thinning can also reduce the cost of later calculations. Otherwise, keep the full run.


Quiz yourself!

Two chains target the same posterior. Their stationary autocorrelations are \(\rho_k=0.9^k\) for chain A and \(\rho_k=0.3^k\) for chain B. If you can afford 10,000 iterations, which chain gives the more precise estimate of the posterior mean, and roughly by how much?



4.3.3 Bias and variation are different problems
Starting a chain far from the region where most posterior values lie can pull its estimated mean toward the starting value. This is initialization bias. Discarding enough early values can reduce this effect.
Even after the starting point has little influence, repeated simulations give different estimates. This is Monte Carlo variation. Retaining more draws generally reduces that variation, although strongly dependent draws improve precision more slowly than independent draws.
These two sources of error are related. A longer run can also reduce the influence of the starting point, because the early values make up a smaller share of the average. But running longer only helps if the chain explores the posterior: A chain that misses an important region can give a very precise estimate of the wrong answer (Margossian & Gelman, 2026).
We can see both effects by repeating the Normal simulation from the fixed starting value 6, using \(\phi=0.99\). In Figure 4.6 we vary how many early states we discard and how many later states we retain. Each panel contains the estimated means from 200 runs.








Figure 4.6: Repeated estimates of the mean of a standard Normal target, using an AR(1) chain with phi = 0.99 started at 6. Each panel contains 200 independent runs. The dashed line is the exact mean, zero. Discarding more initial states reduces the displacement of the estimates; retaining more states reduces their spread.





In the upper panels, early values near 6 pull the estimates above zero. Discarding 500 states largely removes that shift. Compare the columns as well: Retaining 2,000 states gives a narrower spread of estimates than retaining 200. Burn-in addresses the influence of initialization; more retained values improve precision once the chain is exploring the target satisfactorily.
A small MCSE answers the precision question. It does not establish that initialization bias is negligible or that the chain has visited every important region. We therefore need to compare chains as well as assess the precision within a run.


Quiz yourself!

A fit reports a posterior mean of \(12.4\) with posterior standard deviation \(3.0\) and \(N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 36\). What is the MCSE of the posterior mean? How would you communicate its numerical uncertainty? How many effective draws would give a mean MCSE of \(0.05\)?

title: 4  Diagnosing Markov Chains
text:
4.4 Comparing several chains
A single chain cannot reveal that another starting point would lead to a different answer. Several chains let us make that comparison. If they explore the same distribution sufficiently well, their means and ranges should be similar. Persistent differences are a reason to investigate.
Consider two sets of four records in Figure 4.7. In the first set, every record consists of standard Normal draws. In the second, two records fluctuate around \(-2\) and two around \(2\), each with standard deviation one. These illustrate agreement and disagreement about location. Each matrix below has 1,000 rows and four columns, one column per record. We create the second set by shifting two columns down by two and two up by two.

set.seed(48106)
agree <- matrix(rnorm(4000), ncol = 4)
separated <- matrix(rnorm(4000), ncol = 4)
separated[, 1:2] <- separated[, 1:2] - 2
separated[, 3:4] <- separated[, 3:4] + 2









Figure 4.7: Records that agree (left column) and records that disagree about location (right column). Traces show the values over time; density curves summarize the distribution within each record. Each individual record fluctuates rapidly in both sets.





The individual records in both sets have little autocorrelation. That tells us about dependence within each record; it does not tell us whether the records agree with one another. In the second set, pooling the values would hide the fact that no individual record has covered the combined distribution.

4.4.1 The idea behind R-hat
The diagnostic \(\widehat R\), pronounced R-hat, compares variation between chains with variation within chains (Gelman & Rubin, 1992). It is close to one when these give compatible pictures of the distribution, and larger when the chains disagree.
Suppose there are \(m\) chains with \(L=N/m\) retained values each, where \(N\) is the total number of retained values. Write \(\bar\theta_j\) and \(s_j^2\) for the sample mean and sample variance of chain \(j\). The average of the chain variances is \[
W=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}s_j^2.
\] This describes how much values vary within the chains. To compare the chains, calculate the sample variance of their means and multiply it by the chain length: \[
B=\frac{L}{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{m}(\bar\theta_j-\bar\theta_{\cdot})^2,
\qquad
\bar\theta_{\cdot}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\bar\theta_j.
\] Here \(\bar\theta_{\cdot}\) is the average of the chain means. The basic calculation combines \(W\) and \(B\) as \[
\widehat{\operatorname{var}}^{+}=\frac{L-1}{L}W+\frac{B}{L},
\qquad
\widehat R=\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{var}}^{+}}{W}}.
\] The numerator includes differences between the chain means, whereas the denominator describes variation within the chains. Large differences between the means can therefore raise the ratio above one.
Return to the disagreeing records in Figure 4.7, stored in separated. We calculate a mean and a sample variance for each column. colMeans() gives the four means; apply(separated, 2, var) applies var() to each column:

chain_means <- colMeans(separated)
chain_variances <- apply(separated, 2, var)
rbind(mean = chain_means, variance = chain_variances)
#>               [,1]       [,2]      [,3]     [,4]
#> mean     -1.986436 -2.0255178 2.0236908 1.982948
#> variance  1.028308  0.9152197 0.9727786 1.011858

The sample variances are close to one, but they differ because they come from different random draws. Averaging them gives \[
W\approx\frac{1.028+0.915+0.973+1.012}{4}=0.982.
\] The four means are approximately \(-1.986,-2.026,2.024,\) and \(1.983\). We calculate their sample variance and multiply it by \(L=1{,}000\) to obtain \(B\). The code uses the unrounded values for all calculations:

L <- nrow(separated)
W <- mean(chain_variances)
B <- L * var(chain_means)
var_plus <- (L - 1) / L * W + B / L
c(W = W, B = B, rhat = sqrt(var_plus / W))
#>            W            B         rhat 
#>    0.9820411 5358.6838225    2.5408029

With \(B\approx5358.68\), the resulting comparison is \[
\widehat R\approx
\sqrt{\frac{(999/1000)\times0.982+5358.68/1000}{0.982}}
\approx2.541.
\] The records differ much more from one another than their individual variances suggest. The large R-hat makes that disagreement visible in a single number.


4.4.2 Comparing earlier and later values
Whole-chain averages can miss a shared trend. In the upward-trending example in Figure 4.3, all four records rise from a low level to a high level at about the same rate. Their overall means can be similar even though the traces are still changing.
Split R-hat addresses this by dividing each chain into an earlier half and a later half, then treating the halves as separate chains. Four chains become eight half-chains. In the trend example, the earlier halves have lower means than the later halves, so the comparison reveals the change over time.
We can see the difference by regenerating those records. Each column adds the same increasing sequence to small random fluctuations. The two calls to rhat_basic() compare the basic calculation before and after splitting:

set.seed(48104)
L <- 1000
trend <- sapply(1:4, function(j) {
  0.05 + 0.015 * j + seq(0, 0.45, length.out = L) +
    rnorm(L, 0, 0.012)
})
c(basic = rhat_basic(trend, split = FALSE),
  split = rhat_basic(trend, split = TRUE))
#>    basic    split 
#> 1.010852 2.088141

The basic value is about 1.011 despite the obvious upward movement. It is just above the diagnostic target of 1.01, so it gives a weak warning. Splitting raises the value to about 2.088: the difference between the earlier and later halves now produces a much clearer warning.
For practical use, posterior::rhat() performs this split and also checks for differences in spread (Vehtari et al., 2021). It accepts a matrix with one column per chain. Applied to the two sets in Figure 4.7:

c(agreement = posterior::rhat(agree), disagreement = posterior::rhat(separated))
#>    agreement disagreement 
#>    0.9998501    1.7230083

Use \(\widehat R<1.01\) as a diagnostic target for each monitored parameter. A value of 1.04 calls for investigation even if the software uses a looser warning threshold. Inspect the traces and density curves to see what differs. If the chains agree, assess whether their MCSEs are small enough for the quantities you want to report.
Rank normalization compares the ranks of the sampled values, reducing the influence of a few extreme values. Folding compares their distances from a common center. This helps reveal chains that have similar means but different spreads—a disagreement that comparing means alone can miss. Section C.3 explains both calculations.

title: 4  Diagnosing Markov Chains
text:
4.5 A worked analysis: Dutch-language radio
Suppose you want to know what proportion of the songs played on Dutch radio station NPO 3FM are sung in Dutch. Let \(\pi\) denote that proportion. You choose a Beta\((2,5)\) prior and listen to \(n=20\) randomly selected tracks, seven of which are in Dutch. The Beta-Binomial update from Chapter 2 gives \[
\pi\mid y\sim\text{Beta}(9,18).
\] We will estimate its mean and a 95% credible interval by simulation. The exact posterior gives us a useful check on the results. For this analysis, suppose we want the MCSE of the mean and of each interval endpoint to be at most 0.005 on the proportion scale. An MCSE of 0.005 corresponds to half a percentage point in the reported proportion. We will check the mean and both interval endpoints against this tolerance.

4.5.1 Generating the chains with Stan
Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017) generates posterior draws from a model specification. We tell it what is observed, which parameters are unknown, and which prior and likelihood define the model. Its sampling algorithm is explained in Chapter 10 (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo). Here we use it to obtain chains that we can inspect with the tools just developed.
The R package rstan fits a model written in Stan’s language. The model has three blocks: data declares the observations, parameters declares the unknown proportion, and model specifies the prior and likelihood.

radio_model <- "
data {
  int<lower = 0> n;                  // number of tracks sampled
  int<lower = 0, upper = n> y;       // number of tracks in Dutch
}
parameters {
  real<lower = 0, upper = 1> pi;     // proportion of tracks in Dutch
}
model {
  y ~ binomial(n, pi);               // likelihood
  pi ~ beta(2, 5);                   // prior
}
"

Here int means an integer count and real a continuous quantity. The bounds restrict pi to proportions between zero and one. The two statements in model describe the Binomial likelihood and Beta prior; Stan uses them to evaluate the log posterior.
We ask for four chains of 2,000 iterations, discarding the first 1,000 of each as warm-up. The remaining 1,000 values per chain give \(N=4{,}000\) retained draws:

radio_data <- list(n = 20, y = 7)
radio_fit <- stan(model_code = radio_model, data = radio_data,
                  chains = 4, iter = 2000, warmup = 1000,
                  seed = 84735, refresh = 0)

The first call compiles the model before sampling, which can take longer than the simulation itself. as.array() then arranges the retained draws by iteration, chain, and parameter. We select pi, leaving a matrix with one column per chain. The two blank positions in radio_array[, , "pi"] keep every retained iteration and every chain:

radio_array <- as.array(radio_fit)
pi_mat <- radio_array[, , "pi"]
dim(pi_mat)
#> [1] 1000    4

Keep this structure when computing diagnostics. Flattening the matrix into one long vector would lose the chain boundaries.


Quiz yourself!

You call stan() with chains = 3 and iter = 5000, leaving warm-up at its default of half the iterations. How many draws do you retain per chain and in total? What changes if you set warmup = 500?



4.5.2 Do the chains explore similar values?
The bayesplot package provides one function for each graphical check. mcmc_trace() shows movement over time, mcmc_acf() shows dependence within each chain, and mcmc_dens_overlay() draws a density curve for each chain. The argument pars = "pi" selects the proportion we want to examine:

mcmc_trace(radio_array, pars = "pi")
mcmc_acf(radio_array, pars = "pi", lags = 20)
mcmc_dens_overlay(radio_array, pars = "pi")

Figure 4.8 brings these three plots together. Read them as complementary views of the same simulation.








Figure 4.8: The radio posterior from four Stan chains. Top: retained values over time. Bottom left: autocorrelation within each chain. Bottom right: density estimates from the separate chains.





The traces fluctuate through similar ranges, their autocorrelations fall quickly, and the density curves overlap. R-hat provides the corresponding numerical comparison:

posterior::rhat(pi_mat)
#> [1] 1.003033

For this run it is 1.003, below 1.01. We also ask Stan to check for problems specific to its sampling algorithm:

rstan::check_hmc_diagnostics(radio_fit)

Stan reports no such problems for this fit. Chapter 10 (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo) explains these checks in detail. When a fit does produce warnings, investigate them before relying on the posterior summaries.


4.5.3 Is the mean precise enough?
Calculate the posterior mean, posterior standard deviation, and MCSE of the mean:

c(mean = mean(pi_mat), posterior_sd = sd(pi_mat),
  mean_mcse = mcse_mean(pi_mat))
#>         mean posterior_sd    mean_mcse 
#>  0.338817635  0.089925277  0.002332468

The estimated mean is 0.339, with MCSE 0.0023. This meets our target of 0.005. The exact mean is \(9/27=1/3\); the difference between the simulated and exact means is 0.0055, or 2.4 MCSEs.
Keep the two standard deviations separate. The posterior standard deviation, about 0.09, describes uncertainty about the unknown proportion of Dutch-language tracks. The MCSE describes uncertainty in our numerical estimate of the posterior mean. Running the chain longer can reduce the second without changing the first.


4.5.4 Are the interval endpoints precise enough?
A precise mean does not ensure a precise credible interval. The endpoints are the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles: they leave 2.5% of the posterior probability below the interval and 2.5% above it. We need to assess their numerical error separately. mcse_quantile() calculates the MCSE at specified probabilities:

interval_precision <- tibble(
  probability = c(0.025, 0.975),
  estimate = as.numeric(quantile(pi_mat, c(0.025, 0.975))),
  exact = qbeta(probability, 9, 18),
  mcse = as.numeric(mcse_quantile(pi_mat, probs = probability))
)
interval_precision
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   probability estimate exact    mcse
#>         <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1       0.025    0.180 0.172 0.00436
#> 2       0.975    0.522 0.518 0.00458

Each row gives an endpoint estimate, its exact value, and its MCSE. Both MCSEs are below 0.005, so this run also meets our requirement for the interval. The estimated 95% credible interval is [0.18, 0.522]. The MCSEs describe how much its endpoints would change between simulations; they do not describe uncertainty about \(\pi\) itself.
If an endpoint’s MCSE had been 0.01, a run about four times as long would be a reasonable starting plan for reaching 0.005. We would then check both the chain behavior and the achieved precision again. Tail quantiles often need many effective draws because relatively few sampled values lie near the endpoints. There is no single ESS threshold that ensures a chosen decimal precision for every posterior.


4.5.5 Reading bulk and tail ESS in a summary
Software summaries often include ess_bulk and ess_tail. These give broad checks on sampling efficiency in the main body and tails of the distribution (Vehtari et al., 2021). For the radio fit:

c(ess_bulk = ess_bulk(pi_mat), ess_tail = ess_tail(pi_mat))
#> ess_bulk ess_tail 
#> 1482.134 1532.167

Bulk ESS uses the relative ordering of the draws to assess sampling through the main body of the distribution. Tail ESS is the smaller of the ESS estimates for the 5% and 95% quantiles. A large bulk ESS with a small tail ESS is a reason to look more closely at the tails, especially when reporting a credible interval.


Practical diagnostic targets


Aim for R-hat below 1.01 for every monitored parameter.
With four chains, aim for both bulk ESS and tail ESS of at least 400 in total (Vehtari et al., 2021).
Check the MCSE of each summary you intend to report. Meeting the ESS target does not necessarily give enough precision for your purpose.

Use these targets alongside the trace plots and sampler checks. They do not guarantee that every important posterior region has been explored.



4.5.6 What would we report?
Under the Beta-Binomial model, the posterior mean proportion of Dutch-language tracks is approximately 0.34, with a 95% credible interval from 0.18 to 0.52.
R-hat is 1.003, below 1.01. Bulk and tail ESS are 1482 and 1532, both above 400. The MCSEs of the mean and both interval endpoints meet our tolerance of 0.005. Together with the satisfactory plots and absence of Stan sampler warnings, these results give us a reason to stop sampling for the present analysis.
Figure 4.9 compares the simulated distribution with the known posterior. In a more complex model this exact check may be unavailable, but the diagnostic questions remain the same.








Figure 4.9: Histogram of the 4,000 Stan draws for the proportion of Dutch-language tracks, with the exact Beta(9, 18) posterior overlaid.







Choosing the next step


Early values still move away from the starts: consider more warm-up and inspect the new runs.
Chains explore similar values, but the required summaries have large MCSEs: retain more draws or improve mixing.
Chains remain in different regions, or the sampler reports problems: investigate the cause before relying on a longer run.
Plots and diagnostics are satisfactory, and the intended summaries meet their precision targets: report the estimates with their numerical precision.

title: 4  Diagnosing Markov Chains
section: 4.6 What a reassuring run can miss
text:
4.6 What a reassuring run can miss
Agreement over a short interval does not establish that a longer run will behave the same way. Figure 4.10 illustrates a record that looks stable for its first 1,000 values but later moves to a different level.








Figure 4.10: A synthetic example of a late change. The first 1,000 values (left) look stable. The longer run (right) reveals a move to a different level after 3,000 values.





The late change might represent arrival in a region with more posterior probability, or movement between two modes. One jump does not tell us which explanation applies. We need to examine the longer run and, when several modes are present, see whether the chains move between them repeatedly.
Several chains can also agree because they have all missed the same region. Suppose the target is an equal mixture of N\((-3,1)\) and N\((3,1)\). Its mean is zero and half its probability lies on each side of zero. What would we see if every chain stayed near the left mode?
We can illustrate that output with four AR(1) records centered at \(-3\). These sample the left Normal component; they are not samplers for the full mixture. Figure 4.11 compares their output with the whole target.








Figure 4.11: Four records representing exploration of only the left mode of a bimodal posterior. Left: the trace looks healthy and the chains agree. Right: the density estimated from the chains (purple) against the true posterior (gray). The records agree around the left mode, but their estimated mean is near -3 rather than the full posterior mean of zero.





The traces look stable and R-hat is 1.002. Nevertheless, the estimated mean is near \(-3\) rather than zero. Agreement has not revealed the missing mode. An MCSE calculated from these records describes variation within the explored region and misses the much larger error caused by incomplete exploration.
Dispersed starting values help because different chains may find different regions. Knowledge of the model also matters: a mixture model, for example, may suggest several modes worth investigating. Chapter 5 (The Metropolis Algorithm) shows this difficulty with an actual sampler. No diagnostic based only on visited values can tell us everything about a region that was never visited.
A separate question is whether the model describes the observed data well. Even an accurate simulation can represent the posterior of an unsuitable model. Posterior predictive checks address that question by comparing observations simulated from the fitted model with the data.

title: 4  Diagnosing Markov Chains
text:
4.7 Chapter summary
A finite simulation needs both adequate exploration and adequate precision. Trace plots reveal movement over time, and comparisons between chains can expose regions explored from one starting point but not another. Burn-in reduces the influence of initialization; Stan’s warm-up also adjusts its sampling settings.
Autocorrelation explains why a long chain can give an imprecise average. Effective sample size expresses that precision relative to independent draws, and MCSE expresses the numerical uncertainty in the units of the summary. More retained draws generally reduce Monte Carlo variation, but they do not reduce posterior uncertainty about the parameter.
R-hat compares chains and their halves. Use it alongside plots and sampler checks, then assess the MCSE of each mean, probability, or interval endpoint you intend to report. Satisfactory diagnostics support a decision to use the results; they cannot prove that no important region has been missed.

title: 4  Diagnosing Markov Chains
text:
4.8 Quiz answers
Quiz 1. Disagreement between chains. A single chain confined to one mode can produce a stable-looking trace. Additional chains started elsewhere may reveal a different region. Drift and flat stretches can be visible within one chain; comparison between chains requires more than one.
Quiz 2. If the ACF decays geometrically, \(\rho_k = \rho_1^k\), then \(N_{\mathrm{eff}} = N (1 - \rho_1)/(1 + \rho_1)\). Chain A is worth \(10{,}000 \times 0.1 / 1.9 \approx 526\) independent draws and chain B \(10{,}000 \times 0.7 / 1.3 \approx 5{,}385\), about ten times as many. The Monte Carlo standard error of chain B’s posterior mean is therefore about \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\) times smaller.
Quiz 3. The mean MCSE is \(3.0/\sqrt{36}=0.5\). Communicate the estimate with its numerical uncertainty, for example an estimated posterior mean of 12.4 with MCSE 0.5, rather than claiming that its first decimal is stable. A target MCSE of 0.05 requires \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}=(3.0/0.05)^2=3{,}600\), one hundred times as many effective draws. This target does not guarantee stable rounding.
Quiz 4. Each chain runs 5,000 iterations, of which the first 2,500 are warm-up by default, leaving 2,500 draws per chain and \(3 \times 2{,}500 = 7{,}500\) in total. With warmup = 500, only 500 iterations per chain are discarded, so you keep 4,500 per chain and 13,500 in total. Whether 500 is adequate requires checking adaptation, sampler warnings, and the retained chains; a trace alone cannot settle it.

title: 4  Diagnosing Markov Chains
text:
4.9 Exercises

4.9.1 Conceptual exercises

Exercise 4.1 (Warm-up or burn-in?) Explain the difference between burn-in and Stan’s warm-up. Why are adaptation draws excluded even when initialization is near the posterior mode? For a fixed transition rule, distinguish starting at the mode from drawing the initial state from the exact posterior. Which establishes stationarity, and why?


Exercise 4.2 (Thinning by the numbers) A chain of \(N = 20{,}000\) draws has autocorrelations \(\rho_k = 0.9^k\).

Compute its effective sample size.
The chain is thinned by keeping every fifth draw. What are the autocorrelations of the thinned chain, and what is its effective sample size?
A colleague argues that the thinned chain is better because its draws are “almost independent.” Explain what they have confused.



Exercise 4.3 (Four messages) A classmate is running their first Stan models and sends you four messages during the afternoon. Reply to each in two or three sentences, stating what the diagnostic says and what they should do next.

“My \(\widehat{R}\) is 1.00 and the trace plot is a flat band. Am I done?”
“My \(\widehat R\) is 1.04, but the software has not warned me. Does that mean the chains are adequate?”
“My ess_bulk is 3,000 but my ess_tail is 90. I only care about the posterior mean, so can I ignore the tail?”
“My \(\widehat{R}\) is 1.6. I’ll just run the chains ten times longer.”



Exercise 4.4 (How precise is precise enough?) A posterior mean is estimated as \(0.412\) with posterior standard deviation \(0.08\) from a chain with \(N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 250\).

Compute the mean MCSE and give an approximate interval of plus or minus two MCSEs for the numerical uncertainty in the estimated posterior mean. Does this support claiming that its rounding to two decimal places is stable?
How many effective draws are needed to make the MCSE smaller than \(0.001\)?
Explain in one paragraph why increasing \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) shrinks the MCSE but does not shrink the posterior standard deviation, and why a Bayesian should care about the difference.




4.9.2 Practical exercises

Exercise 4.5 (Diagnose these chains) Figure 4.12 shows trace plots of four sets of chains, labelled A to D, and Figure 4.13 shows the corresponding density overlays. The patterns are subtler than the ones in Figure 4.3. For each set, decide whether the chains look healthy, and if not, name the pathology and the diagnostic that reveals it most clearly. Then say, for each unhealthy set, what further information would be needed to judge whether a longer run would help. The records illustrate patterns; do not assume that their generating rules are valid posterior samplers.








Figure 4.12: Trace plots for Exercise 4.5.













Figure 4.13: Density overlays for Exercise 4.5.







Exercise 4.6 (A mixing laboratory) Use ar1_chain() from this chapter.

For \(\phi \in \{0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 0.99\}\), simulate a chain with \(N=20{,}000\) stored states, including its initial state, and compute ess_basic(). Draw that initial state from N\((0,1)\) to isolate dependence from initialization. Plot the effective sample size against \(\phi\) and add the curve \(N(1-\phi)/(1+\phi)\).
For \(\phi = 0.99\), plot the trace of the first 1,000 iterations. Describe what you see and relate it to the effective sample size you computed.
For each \(\phi\), compute the MCSE of the posterior mean using mcse_mean(). Since the true mean is zero, compare the MCSE with the actual error \(|\bar\theta - 0|\) of each chain. Repeat the simulation with a few seeds. Is the MCSE an honest description of the error?



Exercise 4.7 (\(\widehat{R}\) by hand; optional) Optional extension: Use rhat_by_hand() and split_halves() from Section C.2.

Simulate four records of \(N=1{,}000\) stored states from ar1_chain() with \(\phi=0.95\), each started at init=0. Compute unsplit and split basic R-hat by hand. Compare them with rhat_basic(split=FALSE) and rhat_basic(split=TRUE), and also report posterior::rhat(). Are these fixed-start records stationary at time zero?
Now start the four chains at \(-10, -5, 5\), and \(10\). Repeat the same comparisons. Then discard the first 200 iterations of each chain and compute them again. Explain what changed.
Construct four chains that have the same mean but where two chains have three times the spread of the other two, as in Section C.3. Compare rhat_basic() and posterior::rhat() and identify any difference in the values relative to 1.01, and explain which of the two ingredients of the rank-normalized \(\widehat{R}\), rank normalization or folding, is responsible.




4.9.3 Applied exercises

Exercise 4.8 (An undercooked bicycle counter) A bicycle counter on Amsterdam’s Weesperstraat records 23, 19, 25, 21, and 17 bicycles in five one-minute windows. Assume a constant rate \(\lambda\), with \(Y_i\mid\lambda\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\) and a Gamma\((20,1)\) prior (shape 20, rate 1). The exact posterior is Gamma\((125,6)\).
Write this model in Stan as bikes_model, using an array of observed counts in the data block, array[n] int<lower = 0> y;, and a positive real parameter lambda. Fit it with chains = 4, iter = 60, and seed = 84735.

Run the full diagnostic workflow. Which checks fail? Distinguish warnings about the agreement or precision of the chains from warnings about Stan’s sampling algorithm; Chapter 10 explains the latter in detail.
Fit the model at iter = 60, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200, using the same seed. Record R-hat, bulk ESS, tail ESS, mean MCSE, and sampler warnings. Report the first tested setting with R-hat below 1.01, both ESS values at least 400, no sampler warnings, and satisfactory plots. If needed, extend the schedule. Explain why this is not a universal minimum or a guarantee that every larger setting passes.
Estimate \(P(\lambda>22\mid y)\) with an indicator average: give each draw value one if \(\lambda>22\) and zero otherwise, then average. Apply mcse_mean() to this indicator matrix to assess numerical precision, keeping one column per chain. Use a pilot run to plan a run with indicator MCSE at most 0.0025, then check the achieved MCSE and diagnose the final fit. Compare the result with the exact Gamma-posterior probability. Explain why this numerical tolerance does not guarantee stable two-decimal rounding.



Exercise 4.9 (Gen X at the MoMA) The moma_sample data in the bayesrules package records, for a random sample of 100 artists represented in the Museum of Modern Art in New York, whether each was born in the Generation X years or later (the variable genx). Let \(\pi\) be the proportion of such artists in the museum’s collection.

Choose a Beta prior for \(\pi\) that reflects your own expectation, and justify it in one sentence.
Write the Beta-Binomial model in Stan and fit it with four chains. Run the full diagnostic workflow and report \(\widehat{R}\), ess_bulk, ess_tail, and the MCSE of the posterior mean.
Compare the Stan posterior with the exact Beta posterior, both graphically and by posterior mean and 95% credible interval. Are the differences within what the MCSE leads you to expect?
Fit the model again from four dispersed values strictly inside \((0,1)\); the endpoints are not valid finite initial values on Stan’s unconstrained scale. Does anything in the diagnostics change? Should it?

Appendix A — Software Setup
text:
A.1 R and RStudio
Everything in this book runs in R. Most of it needs nothing beyond a handful of CRAN packages, because the point of the book is that you write the samplers yourself. The one exception is Stan, which we use in Chapter 4 and Chapter 10 (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo), and which needs a C++ compiler on your machine. This appendix walks you through the installation in the order that causes the fewest problems, gives you a small model to confirm that Stan works, and tells you what to do if it does not.
If you took the Bayesian Statistics course on this machine, you probably already have everything. Skip to Section A.4 and run the test model; if it passes, you are done.
Install R first and RStudio second; RStudio is an editor and needs R to be there already.
Both are free. Quarto, which we use to build this book, ships inside RStudio; you do not need it for the course.

title: Appendix A — Software Setup
text:
R (4.4 or later). Download the installer for your operating system from cran.r-project.org. On macOS, pick the build that matches your processor (Apple silicon or Intel). If you already have R, check its version with R.version.string and upgrade if it is older than 4.4, because several packages we use no longer support older versions.
RStudio. Download RStudio Desktop from posit.co. Any recent version is fine.

title: Appendix A — Software Setup
text:
A.2 R packages
The packages below cover the whole book. Copy this block into the R console and run it once. It downloads binaries on macOS and Windows and takes a few minutes; on Linux it compiles from source and takes longer.

install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",   # data handling and plots
  "bayesrules",  # data sets from Bayes Rules!
  "bayesplot",   # trace plots and other MCMC graphics
  "posterior",   # effective sample size, R-hat, draws objects
  "coda",        # classic MCMC diagnostics
  "mvtnorm",     # multivariate Normal densities and draws
  "patchwork",   # combining ggplot2 figures
  "rstan",       # Stan
  "bgms",        # Bayesian graphical models, Chapters 7-9
  "lars"         # the diabetes data, Chapters 8-9
))

rstan is on CRAN like the others, and on macOS and Windows it installs as a pre-built binary without compiling anything. That is the easy half. The hard half is that using rstan means compiling each Stan model into C++ the first time you run it, and for that your machine needs a C++ toolchain. The next section installs it.

title: Appendix A — Software Setup
text:
A.3 Installing Stan
rstan is the R interface to Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017). The Stan program you write is translated to C++ and compiled, so you need a compiler that R knows how to call. What that means depends on your operating system.
macOS. Install the Xcode Command Line Tools by opening the Terminal app and running
xcode-select --install
A dialog asks you to confirm; the download is a few gigabytes and takes a while. You do not need the full Xcode application from the App Store. If you already have the tools, the command says so and you can move on.
Windows. Install Rtools from CRAN, choosing the version that matches your R version: Rtools 4.4 for R 4.4.x, Rtools 4.5 for R 4.5.x, and so on. The CRAN download page for Windows lists them under “Rtools”. Accept the default installation location. A mismatch between the Rtools version and the R version is the most common reason that Stan will not compile on Windows, so check R.version.string before you download.
Linux. You need g++ and make, which on Debian and Ubuntu come with the build-essential package, plus the R development headers (r-base-dev). install.packages("rstan") then compiles rstan and its dependencies from source, which takes ten to twenty minutes. The Stan website, mc-stan.org, has distribution-specific notes.
On all three platforms, restart R after installing the toolchain, and confirm that R can see it:

pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)

The answer should be TRUE. If it is FALSE, the toolchain is not installed or R cannot find it, and no Stan model will compile until that is fixed; on Windows, an Rtools version mismatch shows up here.


Two settings worth putting in every Stan script


library(rstan)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())   # run the chains in parallel
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)              # keep the compiled model on disk

The first line runs one chain per processor core instead of one after the other. The second saves the compiled C++ next to your Stan file so that the same model is not recompiled every time you fit it. Both are the settings Bayes Rules! uses, and every Stan chunk in this book assumes them.

section: A.5 If rstan will not compile
text:
A.5 If rstan will not compile
On some machines, most often a managed university laptop or a very new operating system that CRAN’s binaries do not yet target, rstan installs fine but refuses to compile any model, and the error message does not point to a fix. Rather than lose an afternoon, switch to cmdstanr. It is a second R interface to the same Stan, developed by the Stan team, that talks to a separate CmdStan installation instead of compiling inside R’s own toolchain. It is less convenient to install but more robust once it runs.
cmdstanr is not on CRAN. Install it from the Stan team’s R-universe repository, let it repair the toolchain, and then let it download and build CmdStan:

install.packages("cmdstanr",
                 repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev", getOption("repos")))
library(cmdstanr)
check_cmdstan_toolchain(fix = TRUE)   # installs what the compiler is missing, if it can
install_cmdstan(cores = 2)            # downloads and builds CmdStan; several minutes
cmdstan_version()                     # a version number means it worked

On Windows, check_cmdstan_toolchain(fix = TRUE) also needs Rtools, so install that first. On macOS it needs the Xcode Command Line Tools, so the previous section still applies; what cmdstanr sidesteps is the integration between the compiler and R’s own build settings, which is where rstan usually fails.
All Stan code in this book is written for rstan, and translating it takes two lines. Where the book writes

fit <- stan(model_code = bb_model, data = bb_data, chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 84735)

you instead compile and sample in two steps:

mod <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(bb_model))
fit <- mod$sample(data = bb_data, chains = 4, iter_warmup = 1000, iter_sampling = 1000, seed = 84735)

Note that cmdstanr counts warm-up and sampling iterations separately, while rstan’s iter includes warm-up (by default, the first half). Everything after sampling can be the same, because the posterior and bayesplot packages work with both kinds of fit. To get a draws object that the book’s diagnostic code can use:

draws <- posterior::as_draws_array(as.array(fit))   # rstan
draws <- fit$draws()                                # cmdstanr

From here on, posterior::summarise_draws(draws) and bayesplot::mcmc_trace(draws) behave identically. If you use cmdstanr, fit$summary() plays the role of print(fit), and fit$draws(format = "df") gives you the draws as a data frame.

title: Appendix A — Software Setup
text:
A.6 Reproducibility: seeds and sessions
Every method in this book is a simulation, so running the same code twice gives different numbers unless you fix the random number generator. Two seeds matter.
R’s seed. set.seed() fixes the state of R’s random number generator, so that every rnorm(), runif(), and sample() call that follows is reproducible. The book sets set.seed(84735) at the top of every chapter, a nod to Bayes Rules!. Set it once, at the top of your script, not before every sampler call: re-seeding inside a loop gives you the same “random” numbers again and again.
Stan’s seed. Stan runs outside R and has its own generator, so set.seed() does not reach it. Pass seed = to stan() (or to $sample() in cmdstanr), as the test model above does. With the same seed, the same model, the same data, and the same number of chains, Stan produces the same draws, though not necessarily across different Stan versions or operating systems.

set.seed(84735)
x <- rnorm(3)
set.seed(84735)
identical(x, rnorm(3))

[1] TRUE


Reproducible does not mean correct. A seed makes a bug repeatable, which is useful for finding it, but when you want to know whether a sampler works, run it with several seeds and check that the conclusions do not change. Chapter 4 makes this idea precise.
Finally, when you report a problem or hand in an assignment, include the output of sessionInfo(). It lists your R version, your operating system, and the version of every loaded package, which is usually the first thing anyone helping you will ask for.

sessionInfo()



Setup checklist


R 4.4 or later, and RStudio.
The package block above, run once.
A C++ toolchain: Xcode Command Line Tools (macOS), Rtools matching your R version (Windows), or build-essential (Linux).
The Beta-Binomial test model compiles and reports a posterior mean for pi near 0.67.
If step 4 fails: cmdstanr from the Stan R-universe, check_cmdstan_toolchain(fix = TRUE), install_cmdstan().
Seeds: set.seed() for R, seed = for Stan; sessionInfo() when asking for help.

title: Appendix B — Notation
text:
B.1 Conventions
This appendix collects the symbols used throughout the book. We follow Bayes Rules! (Johnson et al., 2022) wherever it has a convention, so that nothing you learned there has to be unlearned, and add the symbols that Markov chains and samplers need.
Every density is \(f\). The prior, the likelihood, the posterior, and the density of a proposal are all written \(f(\cdot)\), and the arguments tell you which one is meant: \(f(\theta)\) is the prior, \(f(y \mid \theta)\) the likelihood, and \(f(\theta \mid y)\) the posterior. We do not use \(p(\cdot)\) or \(\pi(\cdot)\) for densities, because \(\pi\) is a proportion parameter in Bayes Rules! and \(\mathbf{p}\) is a momentum in Chapter 10 (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo). When a chapter builds a sampler for a generic target, that target is written \(f(\theta)\), and you should read it as “the posterior, up to a constant we cannot compute.”
Work on the log scale. Every sampler in this book takes a function that returns \(\log f(\theta)\), never \(f(\theta)\), and the code calls it log_target or log_posterior. The reason is numerical: a likelihood of 2,000 observations is a product of 2,000 small numbers and underflows to zero, while its logarithm is a sum of 2,000 moderate numbers. On the log scale a ratio becomes a difference, \(\log r = \log f(\theta^\star) - \log f(\theta^{(t)})\), and the acceptance test becomes \(\log u < \log r\) (Chapter 5 (The Metropolis Algorithm)). R’s d* functions all take log = TRUE for exactly this purpose.
Vectors are bold, indices are subscripts, iterations are superscripts. A single parameter is \(\theta\); a vector of parameters is \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_d)\); a matrix is a bold capital such as \(\mathbf{P}\) or \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). Observations are indexed \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), predictors \(j = 1, \ldots, p\), and models \(m = 1, \ldots, M\). The state of a Markov chain at iteration \(t\) is \(\theta^{(t)}\), with parentheses so that it is not mistaken for a power; a proposed value is \(\theta^\star\). Chains start at \(t = 0\) and run for \(t = 1, \ldots, T\) iterations. Hats denote estimates computed from draws, as in \(\widehat{R}\).

title: Appendix C — Technical Notes on MCMC Diagnostics
text:
C.1 The variance of a dependent average
These notes give the derivations and diagnostic implementations used in Chapter 4. Exercise 4.7 uses the R-hat functions in Section C.2.
For \(N\) independent draws, the variance of their average is \(\sigma^2/N\). With dependent draws, the covariances also contribute. For a stationary chain, \(\operatorname{Cov}(\theta^{(t)},\theta^{(t+k)})=\sigma^2\rho_k\). There are \(N-k\) pairs of values separated by lag \(k\), giving \[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar\theta)
=\frac{\sigma^2}{N}\left[1+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}
\left(1-\frac{k}{N}\right)\rho_k\right].
\tag{C.1}\] This expression is exact for a stationary chain with finite variance. When \(N\) is large relative to the lags with appreciable correlation, the weights \(1-k/N\) are close to one. Extending the sum gives the large-\(N\) approximation used in Chapter 4: \[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar\theta)\approx\frac{\sigma^2}{N}
\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\rho_k\right).
\]
Positive autocorrelation increases this variance. Negative autocorrelation can reduce it: for example, the AR(1) formula gives \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}>N\) when \(\phi<0\). Thinning such a chain can remove the benefit of its negative autocorrelation.
Bias and variation can also be combined in one expression. For an estimate \(\widehat\mu\) of a mean \(\mu\), \[
\mathbb E[(\widehat\mu-\mu)^2]
=\bigl(\mathbb E[\widehat\mu]-\mu\bigr)^2
+\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu).
\tag{C.2}\] The mean squared error on the left is the sum of squared bias and Monte Carlo variance. Bias describes a systematic displacement from the true mean; Monte Carlo variance describes how much the estimates vary between runs (Margossian & Gelman, 2026).

title: Appendix C — Technical Notes on MCMC Diagnostics
section: C.2 Calculating basic and split R-hat
text:
C.2 Calculating basic and split R-hat
For \(m\) chains of length \(L\), let \(s_j^2\) and \(\bar\theta_j\) be the variance and mean within chain \(j\), and \(\bar\theta_{\cdot}\) the average of the chain means. Then \[
W=\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m s_j^2,\qquad
B=\frac{L}{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^m(\bar\theta_j-\bar\theta_{\cdot})^2.
\] We illustrate the calculation with four records of independent standard Normal draws. The following functions implement the basic R-hat formula and split each column into equal-length first and last halves. For an odd number of values, the middle value is left out.

rhat_by_hand <- function(x) {
  L <- nrow(x)
  W <- mean(apply(x, 2, var))
  B <- L * var(colMeans(x))
  sqrt(((L - 1) / L * W + B / L) / W)
}
split_halves <- function(x) {
  half <- floor(nrow(x) / 2)
  cbind(x[seq_len(half), , drop = FALSE],
        x[seq.int(nrow(x) - half + 1, nrow(x)), , drop = FALSE])
}
set.seed(48407)
normal_chains <- matrix(rnorm(4000), ncol = 4)
rbind(
  unsplit = c(by_hand = rhat_by_hand(normal_chains),
              package = rhat_basic(normal_chains, split = FALSE)),
  split = c(by_hand = rhat_by_hand(split_halves(normal_chains)),
            package = rhat_basic(normal_chains, split = TRUE))
)
#>          by_hand  package
#> unsplit 1.000113 1.000113
#> split   1.000048 1.000048

Within each row, the hand and package calculations match because they implement the same formula. The split and unsplit results can also look nearly identical after rounding when both halves explore similar values. rhat_basic() splits by default; split = FALSE disables that step.

title: Appendix C — Technical Notes on MCMC Diagnostics
text:
C.3 Rank normalization and folding
Chains can agree about their center and still disagree about their spread. Suppose two records vary narrowly around zero while two others range much farther above and below it. Their means can be similar, so comparing means alone may give little warning.
The following code creates that situation. All four records have an expected mean of zero, but the last two have standard deviation three instead of one:

set.seed(48408)
same_mean <- cbind(rnorm(1000, 0, 1), rnorm(1000, 0, 1), rnorm(1000, 0, 3), rnorm(1000, 0, 3))
c(basic = rhat_basic(same_mean), rank_normalized = posterior::rhat(same_mean))
#>           basic rank_normalized 
#>        1.000529        1.187145

posterior::rhat() adds two improvements to the basic split calculation (Vehtari et al., 2021).
Rank normalization replaces values by their positions in an ordered list. For example, the values \((-3,-1,1,3)\) have ranks \((1,2,3,4)\). An extremely large value still receives the highest rank, but its numerical size no longer dominates the comparison.
After splitting the chains, we rank all their retained values together. Ties receive their average rank. We then convert the ranks to standard Normal scores. If \(r\) is a rank and \(S\) the total number of ranked values, the transformation is \[
z=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{r-3/8}{S+1/4}\right).
\] The expression inside \(\Phi^{-1}\) turns a rank into a probability between zero and one; \(\Phi^{-1}\) gives the corresponding standard Normal quantile. For the four-value example, the scores are approximately \((-1.05,-0.30,0.30,1.05)\). We calculate basic R-hat on the scores. This makes the comparison less sensitive to extreme values, including those from distributions with very long tails. Bulk ESS uses this same transformation of the split chains before estimating ESS. Tail ESS instead computes ESS for indicators of falling below the pooled 5% quantile and below the pooled 95% quantile, and reports the smaller value.
Folding checks spread more directly. Replace each original value by its distance from the pooled median. In the four-value example the median is zero, so \((-3,-1,1,3)\) becomes \((3,1,1,3)\). The sign disappears and distance from the center remains. Wider chains now tend to have larger values than narrower chains. We split and rank-normalize these distances, then calculate R-hat again.
The reported posterior::rhat() is the larger of these two results. Figure C.1 shows how folding separates records with different spreads. In this example, ranking the original values alone can miss the problem, while folding reveals it. The code below calculates both parts and compares their maximum with posterior::rhat():

rank_normalize <- function(x) {
  ranks <- rank(x, ties.method = "average")
  scores <- qnorm((ranks - 3/8) / (length(ranks) + 1/4))
  matrix(scores, nrow = nrow(x), ncol = ncol(x))
}
rank_component <- rhat_by_hand(rank_normalize(split_halves(same_mean)))
folded <- abs(same_mean - median(same_mean))
fold_component <- rhat_by_hand(rank_normalize(split_halves(folded)))
c(rank_component = rank_component, folded_component = fold_component,
  maximum = max(rank_component, fold_component), package = posterior::rhat(same_mean))
#>   rank_component folded_component          maximum          package 
#>         1.000340         1.187145         1.187145         1.187145
